title: Equal in the Eyes of Hashem

article.body:
Rochel reached over and stroked her daughter’s cheek. “Excellent question, Devorah Leah’le. Your question shows me you listened very well.

that there is nothing greater than simple emunah in Hashem. Simple emunah that Hashem created the world, and that He runs it with chessed and rachamim, is planted in the neshama of every Yid. And whenever Yidden with that emunah daven to Hashem with a full heart, their tefillah is answered—even if they don’t understand the sheimos they are saying. Only a very unusual and

great miracle needs to be done by tzaddikim like the Baal Shem.

like a father who provides for his young children. When the child needs something—maybe he’s hungry and wants some food, or maybe he needs new shoes—the child doesn’t need to use any fancy words to ask for it. He can just say, “Tatte, please give me what I lack,” and the father will give it happily. It is only if the child wants something out of the ordinary that he would have to use different words to convince his father to give it to him. And he might even ask someone older, like his father’s friend, to help him.

when we need a miracle that is out of the ordinary, that that the special kavanos of a ba'al shem are needed.

shem and the mekubalim love all Yidden. Especially simple Yidden. The ones who keep

mitzvos as carefully as they could, even if they don’t know the reasons behind them, and daven carefully every day, even if they don’t understand the words. Zeide Baruch would say that the yiras Shamayim of our neighbor, Leib Shaul the wagon-driver, was greater than the Torah knowledge of Reb Shlomo Leib, a famous iluy from Prague.

LAST TIME: In the evenings, Rochel starts to teach her daughter Torah, as well as stories of their family and Reb Yoel Baal Shem. One night, Devorah Leah asks what the purpose of davening is for simple Jews, who don’t understand the kabbalah behind the names of Hashem. Equal in the Eyes

do with why the mekubalim believe in teaching their daughters Torah. You see, the mekubalim believe that actions done with sincerity and yiras Shamayim are valuable, no matter

who does them. It doesn’t matter if the person is a simple Yid or a talmid chacham, old or young, man or woman. They are all equal in the eyes of Hashem. And so, it makes sense that they believe in teaching their daughters as much as their sons.

think differently. They believe that Torah shouldn’t be taught to everyone. Kabbalah should be hidden, and only taught to a select few scholars. And Torah, in general, should not be taught to women and girls.”

Devorah Leah looked forward to her learning sessions all day. As she hung up the laundry,

scrubbed the dishes, and changed the sheets, she would go over in her mind what she’d learned the night before, over and over again. She didn’t want to forget even a word of it.

Devorah Leah also hoped that now she’d have something to talk about with Baruch. Lately, her younger brother rarely spoke about anything besides Torah learning, which meant that he hardly talked to her at all. Now that she, too, was learning Torah, she hoped to break the ice between them.

She tried for the first time one evening, a few months after she’d started learning. Baruch was waiting for their father to be ready to leave for the beis midrash. The boy was sitting on the porch with his Gemara open, not wanting to waste even a moment. Devorah Leah, glancing

through the window, realized that she recognized the Mishna in the middle of the page. It was exactly the one she was learning with her mother!

Devorah Leah went outside and tapped her brother’s chair. “Baruch.”

politely. After a pause, he added, “And I trust you and Mamme

Baruch frowned, not looking up. “You’ll have to excuse me, please. I’m in the middle, and I don’t want to interrupt.”

would know the answer to,” Devorah Leah smiled shyly. “It’s about…”

Devorah Leah’s voice trailed off; she could tell that her brother was no longer listening.

night, she told her mother of her frustrations with Baruch.
